implementation_notes: Scala has no inline keyword; the JIT (HotSpot) decides, with the same monomorphic-call-site rule as Java - a hot small method is inlined, a megamorphic virtual call is not. The Scala-specific tool is by-name parameters and the ScalaRunTime / specialised collections: a by-name argument (=>) is passed as a function and, when it is a simple expression that HotSpot can see, the expression is inlined at the call site by the 'escape analysis / by-name' optimisation, so 'if (cond) expensive else cheap' as a by-name argument evaluates only cond. Scala also relies on case classes and vals for locality. On Scala Native and Scala.js the picture differs (Scala.js has no JIT; Scala Native uses LLVM), so a 'the JIT inlines it' assumption does not transfer to those targets.
idiom_name: no inline keyword; HotSpot inlining (monomorphic hot sites) plus by-name parameters for on-demand expression evaluation
pitfalls: There is no inline keyword in Scala; the lever is small hot methods and monomorphic call sites (HotSpot rules), not an annotation.
By-name parameters evaluate their argument only when used - the opposite of by-value, and a by-name parameter used more than once re-evaluates the expression (a real cost).
Scala.js has no JIT and therefore no inlining; Scala Native uses LLVM. A HotSpot-tuned hot path does not transfer to those targets.
A megamorphic call site stops HotSpot inlining regardless of how small the callee is - make the site monomorphic.
Specialised collections (ScalaRunTime) can defeat inlining by turning a collection op into a generic loop; for a tiny hot collection, a plain array loop is faster.
